paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Sodium chloride, with the formula NaCl, is an ionic compound made of sodium ions and chloride ions in a 1:1 ratio. It is transparent or translucent and brittle. In nature it turns up as the mineral halite.

paragraphs.heading: Far more than table salt
paragraphs.text: In its edible form, table salt, it seasons food and keeps it from spoiling. Yet the world made roughly 250 million tonnes of it a year according to 2008 data, and the dominant uses are chemicals and de-icing. Making chemicals, directly or indirectly, takes most of the world's production. Salt is a major source of the sodium and chlorine compounds that industry uses as raw material for further chemical synthesis.

paragraphs.heading: Chlorine and sodium hydroxide
paragraphs.text: One key industrial step is an electrolysis run in one of three cell types: mercury, diaphragm or membrane. Each type separates the chlorine from the sodium hydroxide in its own way. Chlorine goes into PVC plastics, disinfectants and solvents, while sodium hydroxide helps industries make paper, soap and aluminium. The electrolysis uses a lot of energy, so new technologies are being developed, as even small gains in efficiency can pay back handsomely.

paragraphs.heading: Other chemical routes
paragraphs.text: In the Solvay process, sodium chloride is turned into sodium carbonate and calcium chloride. Sodium carbonate in turn goes into glass, sodium bicarbonate, dyes and many other chemicals. In the Mannheim process, salt yields sodium sulfate and hydrochloric acid. Because salt is used so heavily, even its minor applications can consume huge amounts.

paragraphs.heading: Odd jobs for salt
paragraphs.text: In oil and gas drilling, salt makes drilling fluid denser so it can hold back high gas pressure deep in the well. Tanners add it to animal hides to hold back microbes on their undersides. Water softeners use resins to strip out the calcium and magnesium ions of hard water, and those resins are made and recharged with sodium chloride.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping roads clear
paragraphs.text: De-icing and anti-icing of roads is salt's second major use. Before snow falls, roads are ideally coated with brine, a strong solution of salt in water, which stops snow and ice from bonding to the surface. That avoids heavy salting after the snow arrives. Salt or brine stops working below −10 °C (14 °F). The lowest freezing point of a salt-water mix is −21.12 °C (−6.02 °F), at 23.31 wt% of salt.

paragraphs.heading: Smarter mixes and side effects
paragraphs.text: Additives can cut costs. In the US, rock salt was mixed with a carbohydrate solution left over from processing sugar beet, and it stuck to roads about 40% better than rock salt alone. Since it stayed put longer, crews did not need to repeat the treatment as often. But road salt ends up in lakes and rivers, where it could harm water plants and animals by disrupting their osmoregulation.
